en: Reconstructed Text of the *Nagaropamasūtra* According to One of the Manuscript Traditions, namely the Pelliot/Stein Manuscript [Opening Verses] Homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great community of bhikṣus, five hundred bhikṣus in all. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One were to teach the Dharma discourse known as the *Nagaropama-sūtra*. Hearing it, the bhikṣus will preserve it in mind. The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. "Even so, Blessed One," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke thus: "Ānanda, suppose there were a man who had set out on a journey for a long road. He would see a large city, a royal capital, prosperous, flourishing, and filled with many people. It would be well-fortified, with high walls and strong gates, and provided with a moat. It would be full of parks, groves, lotus ponds, and palaces. It would be rich in food, drink, and provisions. It would be free from fear, secure, and without calamity. Having seen that city, the man would think: 'If I were to enter this city, I would find rest and relief from my fatigue. He would then enter the city. Once inside, he would find a house, a palace, or a mansion, well-constructed and spacious. He would find a couch, soft and comfortable, spread with fine cloths. He would find food, drink, and various delicacies. He would find servants, attendants, and companions. He would find safety, security, and freedom from fear. In the same way, Ānanda, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, a layman or laywoman, hears this *Nagaropama-sūtra*, they will understand the path of practice. They will understand the path of cultivation. They will understand the path of liberation. They will understand the path to the cessation of suffering. Just as that man, having entered the city, found rest and relief from his fatigue, so too, Ānanda, when a noble disciple hears this *Nagaropama-sūtra*, they find rest and relief from the fatigue of saṃsāra. They find the city of Nirvāṇa. They find the palace of the Dharma. They find the couch of samādhi. They find the food of wisdom. They find the drink of liberation. They find the servants of mindfulness. They find the security of non-regression. They find the freedom from fear of Māra and the afflictions. Therefore, Ānanda, you should preserve this *Nagaropama-sūtra*. Teach it to others. Write it down. Contemplate its meaning. In this way, you will fulfill your duty to the Tathāgata. [The Buddha then recited verses: "Just as a man traveling a long road, Sees a great city, a royal capital, Prosperous, flourishing, and well-guarded, Filled with parks, groves, and lotus ponds; So too, hearing this *Nagaropama-sūtra*, One finds the city of peace, Nirvāṇa. Resting there, one is freed from fatigue, And attains the bliss of the Dharma. Therefore, preserve this teaching, O Ānanda, Teach it to those who seek the path. May all beings, having heard it, Attain the state beyond all fear. [Conclusion] When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said. Thus ends the *Nagaropama-sūtra*, reconstructed according to the Pelliot/Stein manuscript tradition.
I. Canonical Text:
*Nagaropamasūtra* I.1 Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery—SHT 154 (beginning of manuscript).
It begins here as follows: "The setting was Śrāvastī. Formerly, monks, I [attained] perfect awakening.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Formerly, monks, I [attained] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
While he was still unawakened, alone, having gone into seclusion and withdrawn in meditation, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; that is to say, it is born, it grows old, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn.
And yet, these beings do not understand the escape from beyond old age and death."

They do not understand it as it truly is. Then this occurred to me: "When what exists do aging and death come to be? What is the condition for aging and death? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me the realization of things as they truly are: [the knowledge that] when birth exists, aging and death come to be; birth is the condition for aging and death.

"When birth exists, aging and death come to be; moreover, aging and death have birth as their condition. (NagSū I.5) Then this occurred to me: "What being present does birth come to be? And what is the condition for birth? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are.
"When there is becoming, birth comes to be; and birth has becoming as its condition.

We should note that our reconstructed text here (from the end of 119v6 to the beginning of 120r1) contains many more syllables (*akṣara*) than the physical gap would permit. This is because our reconstruction almost certainly represents a version very close to the original.
We have assumed that the scribe’s eye most likely skipped from the first *yathābhūtasyābhi-* (concluding 119v6) down to *-samaya udapādi* (beginning 120r1).
The reconstructed text is based upon Hoernle no. 149.x.33 [= Or.15009 /670] v1–4 and SHT 154.
Then this occurred to me: "When what exists does existence come to be? And what is the condition for existence?
As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When grasping exists, existence comes to be; grasping is the condition for existence."
Then this occurred to me: "When what exists does grasping come to be? And with what as its condition does grasping arise?
As I reflected thoroughly upon this, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
"When craving exists, grasping comes to be; furthermore, grasping has craving as its condition."

NagSū I.8: This occurred to me: "When what exists does craving come to be? And with what as its condition does craving arise? As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are: "When feeling exists, craving comes to be; and with feeling as its condition, craving arises."

NagSū I.9: This occurred to me: "When what exists does feeling come to be? And with what as its condition does feeling arise? As I attended to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is: "When contact exists, feeling comes to be; feeling has contact as its condition."

NagSū I.10: This occurred to me: "When what exists does contact come to be? And with what as its condition does contact arise? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are: "When the six sense-bases exist, contact comes to be; and with the six sense-bases as its condition, contact arises."

NagSū I.11: This thought occurred to me: "When what exists does the sixfold sense-base come to be? And with what as its condition does the sixfold sense-base arise? As I was reflecting thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When name-and-form exists, the sixfold sense-base comes to be; and with name-and-form as its condition, the sixfold sense-base arises."

Then this occurred to me: "When what exists does name-and-form come to be? With what as its condition does name-and-form arise? As I applied my mind to this with systematic attention, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are: "When consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be; with consciousness as its condition, name-and-form arises."
This occurred to me: "When what exists does consciousness come to be? With what as its condition does consciousness arise?

As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are: "When name-and-form exists, consciousness comes to be; with name-and-form as its condition, consciousness arises."
My mind turns back from consciousness; it does not proceed beyond this.

Namely: conditioned by name-and-form is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping;
conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; and conditioned by birth is old age and death.
Thus arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; such is the origin of this entire great mass of suffering.

Then this occurred to me: "In what being absent do aging and death not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of aging and death occur? As I was reflecting thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are: "When birth is absent, aging and death do not come to be; from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death."

NagSū I.17: This occurred to me: "In what being absent does birth not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of birth occur? As I was reflecting thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are: "When existence is absent, birth does not come to be; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth."

NagSū I.18: This occurred to me: "In what being absent does existence (*bhava*) not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of existence follow? As I was reflecting thoroughly (*yoniśo manasikurvat*), there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtasyābhisamaya*):
"When grasping (*upādāna*) is absent, existence does not come to be; from the cessation of grasping comes the cessation of existence."

NagSū I.19: This occurred to me: "In what being absent does grasping not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of grasping occur? As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are: "When craving is absent, grasping does not come to be; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of grasping."

NagSū I.20: This thought occurred to me: "In the absence of what does craving not arise? Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of craving? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
"In the absence of feeling, craving does not arise; through the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving."

Then this occurred to me: "In what being absent does feeling not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of feeling occur? As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is: "In the absence of contact, feeling does not come to be; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling."

Then this occurred to me: "In the absence of what does contact not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of contact occur? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
"In the absence of the six sense bases, contact does not come to be; from the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases."

NagSū I.23: This occurred to me: "In the absence of what does the sixfold sense-base (*ṣaḍāyatana*) not come to be? Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of the sixfold sense-base? As I applied my mind thoroughly (*yoniśo manasikurvataḥ*), there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtasyābhisamaya*):
"In the absence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the sixfold sense-base does not come to be; through the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the sixfold sense-base."

NagSū I.24: This occurred to me: "In the absence of what does name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) not come to be? Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of name-and-form? As I attended to this with systematic reflection (*yoniśo manasikāra*), there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are: "In the absence of consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form does not come to be; through the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form."

NagSū I.25: This occurred to me: "In the absence of what does consciousness not come to be? Through the cessation of what does the cessation of consciousness occur? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
"In the absence of volitional formations, consciousness does not come to be; through the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases."

NagSū I.26: This thought occurred to me: "In what being absent do the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of the formative forces occur? As I reflected thoroughly (*yoniśo manasikurvat*), there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*):
"When ignorance (*avidyā*) is absent, the formative forces do not come to be; from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the formative forces."
P.S. Bleu 67(1)v2 and SHT 420, folio 7r3 (NidSa, transliteration no. 109) contain the following phrase:
Thus, from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
From the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna*); from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact (*sparśa*); and from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling (*vedanā*).
From the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence;
from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death, as well as sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.

NagSū I.28: This occurred to me: "I have discovered that ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail traversed and followed by the seers of old. (The classical Sanskrit form, which we have used throughout the reconstructed portions of our text.)

It would, of course, be *-kair ṛṣi-*. However, as the MS does not allow space for that many *akṣara*s, we have adopted the form used elsewhere in the Pelliot/Stein MS. See note 9 of the translation for further remarks.

It is just as if a man, wandering through a forested ravine, were to discover an ancient path, an ancient track, an ancient trail frequented and traversed by people of old— he would follow it; following it, he would there see an ancient path, an ancient city, an ancient royal capital.
He would see an ancient path—beautiful, well-watered, delightful, endowed with groves, woods, and lotus ponds—and he would think: "Aha!
This is an ancient path."

cf. next paragraph. NagSū I.30: It would occur to him thus: "What if I were to go and inform the king? Then that man, having gone to the king, would inform him: "May your majesty know this: while wandering here in the forest, on a slope, I saw an ancient [city]."

The ancient road, the ancient path, the ancient track traversed and followed by men of old—I followed it. Following it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, endowed with parks, endowed with groves, and endowed with lotus ponds; auspicious, well-fortified, and delightful. May Your Majesty cause that city to be measured out.

NagSū I.31 Then that king might have that city measured out, and after some time it would become a royal capital— prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants. NagSū I.32 In the same way, monks, I have discovered the ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient road traveled and followed by the seers of old.
In this very way:
What is that ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail, traversed and followed by the seers of old?
It is the noble eightfold path; namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.
Right concentration itself is the eighth.
At least one manuscript (SHT 787 = NidSa transliteration no. 127.2) inserts the following sentence after "itself is the eighth":
This, monks, is that ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail, trodden and followed by the seers of old;
cf. also the citation from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* [V. Näther, C. Vogel].

In this way, I saw birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness; I saw the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the origin of the formative forces, the cessation of the formative forces, and the path leading to the cessation of the formative forces. *Note:

I saw birth; I saw the origin of birth, the cessation of birth, and the practice leading to the cessation of birth. I saw existence; I saw the origin of existence, the cessation of existence, and the practice leading to the cessation of existence. I saw clinging; I saw the origin of clinging, the cessation of clinging... [upādāna] (3v1).

I saw the path leading to cessation; I saw craving, the origin of craving, the cessation of craving, and the path leading to the cessation of craving. I saw contact, the origin of contact, the cessation of contact, and the path leading to the cessation of contact. I saw the six sense bases, the origin of the six sense bases, the cessation of the six sense bases, and the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases. I saw name-and-form... [the origin of name-and-form]...

I saw the arising of name-and-form and the cessation of name-and-form, and I saw the practice leading to the cessation of name-and-form; I saw consciousness, the arising of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, and the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness; I saw volitional formations, the arising of volitional formations... [etc. (cf. P.S. Bleu 77v3, 6;
Small fragments: 693, 1295, and 1297; SHT 157, fragment br1 2 and 787r4–v4.

Having personally realized and fully awakened to these dharmas, I proclaim them to the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen, as well as to the various non-Buddhist ascetics, brahmins, wanderers, and peripatetics.

In this regard, a monk who practices correctly is a successful practitioner; he achieves success in the right method, the Dharma, and the wholesome. Likewise, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman who practices correctly is a successful practitioner.
He attains—realizes—the right method, the Dharma, and the wholesome.
Thus, this holy life (brahmacarya) becomes widespread, prevalent among many people, and expanded, being perfectly and well-proclaimed as far as the realms of gods and humans. (NagSū I.40)
Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Nagaropama-sūtra is completed.

II. Appendix.
The first part of the appendix has been adapted from the Petrovsky manuscript, which is the only extant manuscript that preserves [the text] almost entirely.

That portion of the appendix not found in the Pelliot/Stein manuscript. This is because our reconstruction of the canonical text and appendix is intended to represent a single manuscript tradition (reunited from the London and Paris collections).

The section of the Petrovsky manuscript used for the reconstruction of the appendix is presented in bold. The paragraphing is somewhat arbitrary. NagSū II.1: Furthermore, when the prophecy (vyākaraṇa) comparable to a city had appeared, Brahmā Sanatkumāra—possessing a transcendent complexion—having passed through the night, approached the Blessed One; having approached, [he prostrated] at the feet of the Blessed One...
Having bowed his head in salutation, Brahmā Sanatkumāra stood to one side; standing there to one side before the Blessed One, he spoke this verse.
"Aho! This is knowledge, great knowledge, the destroyer of the poison of the afflictions;
it has been spoken by you, O Great Hero, out of compassion for all living beings who are present here."

This reconstruction is tentative, as there is no means to determine the *akṣara*s immediately preceding *upasthitasya* in Pet. 2r2. At the beginning of this line, approximately seven more *akṣara*s are missing;
however, at least the first six almost certainly belong to the end of the canonical text. SHT 179 provides a different transition from the canonical text.
... thus perfectly elucidated; "The Simile of the City" is the designation for the prophecy that has just been concluded. // //
Then Brahmā Sanatkumāra said:

"There are, worthy sir, in the eastern direction two great rākṣasīs who dwell there, named Candraprabhā and Sūryaprabhā. Each has a retinue of a thousand; they provide protection, guardianship, strength, and well-being for human beings."

For one who dwells in comfort and preserves [the teachings], whether on the road or off the road, in a grove or in an empty dwelling, there are these mantra-words by which the four assemblies— the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— as well as other humans, are drawn forth. They are as follows:
The *vaḍa*, *saraḍa*, *cappuṣa*, *śaraṅgulī*,
and *phāṣa* [are used] for the sake of a pleasant touch and a comfortable state of movement; SHT 176.

Fol. 20v3–21r2 reads: "They maintain a state of dwelling in comfort and ease, whether on the right path or on a wrong path, in a grove or in an empty dwelling, for the four assemblies—of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—and for other human beings. (cappuṣa: SHT 176).
Fol. 21r4 reads *capuṭa*.
NagSū II.3: "I shall perform, O worthy one, the accomplishment, protection, binding, and guardianship of this exposition which is like a city—namely:
*purime*, *kapphe*, *parumele*, *rimele*, *parāpare*, *purāpure*, *kukumati*, *kṣīramati*."

"O worthy one, when Māra the Evil One approaches, these mantra-words should be recited before him:
'The Buddha is supreme; you are not supreme. There is no one more supreme than the Tathāgata. For the Buddha is the supreme one in the world, the unsurpassed King of Dharma.'"
Dharma is supreme; you are not supreme, for there is nothing here superior to Dharma.
Indeed, Dharma is the supreme bliss of the world—dispassion and tranquility.
The Saṅgha is supreme; you are not supreme, for there is nothing here superior to the Saṅgha.
For the Saṅgha is the best in the world, the unsurpassed field of merit.

Furthermore, worthy sir, there was a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin called the "City Simile," and a prophecy called the "Door of Dharma" also occurred for the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni; and for the Tathāgata, Arhat, and [Samyaksaṃbuddha] Kāśyapa...
Even for the Perfectly Awakened One, there was a prophecy named "The Door of Dharma" (NagSū II.6).

Furthermore, for the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened Śākyamuni, [there is the prophecy] arising from his realization, as it truly is, of the knowledge of aging and death, the knowledge of the origin of aging and death, and the knowledge of the cessation of aging and death.

Because of his realization, as it truly is, of the knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death; and likewise, because of his realization, as it truly is, of the knowledge of birth, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations;

and because of his knowledge of the arising of volitional formations, his knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations, and his knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations.

Because of his realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam abhisaṃbodhāt*), [he attained] the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) comparable to a city (*nagaropama*) regarding the knowledge of the practice (*pratipajjñāna*). SHT 154.
Fragm. ev1 reads *-pratipadajñāne* (for *-pratipadājñāne*).
Thus, *jāti* is existence (*bhava*): SHT 154, frags.

Repeating the complete formula for each member of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
NagSū II.7: Therefore, this exposition has the designation "the awakening to the Dharma through the simile of the city. NagSū II.8:
Now, while this exposition through the simile of the city was being spoken, this great trichiliocosm...

The world-system shook, trembled, and quaked; it was agitated, violently agitated, and thoroughly agitated; it was distressed, violently distressed, and thoroughly distressed; it moved, trembled, and quaked. (Pet. 5v4 reads in a somewhat different order:)
It was shaken, thoroughly shaken; it moved, thoroughly moved, thoroughly stirred; it trembled, thoroughly trembled, thoroughly agitated; it quaked, thoroughly quaked, thoroughly convulsed.
Therefore, friends, this exposition of the simile of the city must be approved by the monks as being from the Teacher himself.

This exposition must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped; having relied upon it, one should dwell [in accordance with it]. For monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, and piśācas, this exposition must be accepted as the Teacher himself; it must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped.
Having relied upon this, it should be honored and dwelled in.

Furthermore, friends, this exposition likened to a city has been spoken of and rejoiced in by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods of the desire realm; it has also been spoken of and rejoiced in by twenty-eight yakṣa generals.

It was spoken and approved by the four Great Kings; it was spoken and approved by Śakra, Lord of the Devas; it was spoken and approved by Brahmā, the Lord of the Assembly; it was spoken and approved by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Śuddhāvāsa deities; and it was [spoken and approved] by those of the past, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.

It has been spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, will also speak it; and the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One, has also spoken it now in the present time.

NagSū II.11: "O worthy ones, whoever shall recite, retain, cause others to grasp, read, study, master, and attend to this exposition, he shall not be bitten by a snake; [his] poison [shall not take effect]."
Weapons shall not prevail against his body; he shall not die by water; he shall not be burned by fire;
even kings shall not overcome him; thieves shall not rob him. Even when in the midst of a royal court, he shall emerge in safety;
though bound in tight fetters, he shall be released; and even when surrounded by enemies, he shall find himself in an open space—all this shall come to pass for him.

Furthermore, all magical spells, *kākhorda* rites, mantras, and *vetāḍa* demons will depart, and no hosts of spirits will cause harm, except as a result of past karma. Having understood this, Brahmā Sanatkumāra bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One,

NagSū II.27: Having spoken this, the four Great Kings bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and vanished right there.

Then, at the end of that very night, the Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, today, when the night had advanced, Brahmā Sanatkumāra, of surpassing beauty, approached me."

Having prostrated with his head at my feet, Brahmā Sanatkumāra stood to one side; standing to one side, he spoke this verse before me: "O, the knowledge, the great knowledge... as before, up to *NagSū II.29*. He approached them:

Having each taken their respective directions and stood to one side— [the feminine form *sthitā* is to be read instead of *sthitah*]— NagSū II.31: having spoken this, the four great kings bowed their heads at my feet and circumambulated me three times.

Having vanished right there, [the Buddha said]: "Receive it, monks! Retain this 'City-like' Prophecy, preserve it, cause others to grasp it, recite it, master it, and attend to it with the mind. Why is that? Because this 'City-like' Prophecy is endowed with meaning and endowed with the Dharma; it conduces to the higher knowledge of the beginning of the holy life, to full awakening, and to Nirvāṇa."
